questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman was reviewed in the intensive care with fever and hemodynamic instability. She was recently repatriated to a rehabilitation hospital in the United States from India, where she had been hospitalized for 3 months because of a cerebrovascular accident. She had a peripherally inserted central catheter for blood work, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube for supplemental alimentation, and an indwelling urinary catheter. Five days earlier, she had developed fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. She was started on meropenem and fluconazole. Investigations: PICC and peripheral blood cultures: positive for Candida haemulonii after 72 hours; susceptibility as follows: Agent Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) or Mean Effective Concentration (MEC) Interpretation Fluconazole 128 μg/mL Resistant Amphotericin B 2 μg/mL Resistant Micafungin 0.5 μg/mL Susceptible
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely correct identification of the organism?
questions.explanation: Candida auris Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen that causes otomycosis and invasive candidiasis. It is an important nosocomial pathogen, especially in some parts of the world where it has already established endemicity. Healthcareassociated outbreaks have been reported in the United States. C. auris will be misidentified by commercial identification systems. The Vitek-2 will usually misidentify C. auris as Candida haemulonii and sometimes as Candida famata; the API-20C system will misidentify C. auris as Rhodotorula glutinis, Candida sake, or Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The correct identification can be made through DNA sequencing or with matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q25

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man was seen with a history of intermittent fevers over 6 weeks. He denied any other symptoms. He was being investigated for raised blood sugars and had a dental extraction 7 days earlier. He drank 35 units of alcohol per week. He returned from Malaysia 6 months ago following a 2-month stay with his family during the summer months. On examination, his temperature was 38.9°C, and he had mild abdominal tenderness in his right upper quadrant. Investigations: Total white cell count 17.2 ×109/L CRP 230 mg/L Alanine transaminase 152 U/L Alkaline phosphatase 341 U/L Urgent abdominal USS revealed a single large lesion in the right lobe of the liver consistent with an abscess. No biliary pathology was identified. He was commenced on fluids and IV co-amoxiclav Blood cultures – no growth at 5 days Liver aspirate MCS – mucoid colonies on blood and MacConkey agar. The organism did not react with oxidase or indole A B
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae K. pneumoniae (K1 capsular serotype) is an emerging pathogen causing liver abscesses in the absence of hepatobiliary disease. It is found in SE Asia, in particular Malaysia. K. pneumoniae are oxidase-negative, lactose fermenting organism. The hypermucoviscous variant grows as very mucoid colonies and can be identified by a positive string test (stretching colonies forms a “string” of >5mm). E. coli is a common causes of liver abscess, and the culture results would fit (although most E. coli are indole positive) but in the absence of hepatobiliary pathology and sterile blood cultures this would be unlikely. E. histolytica commonly presents as an indolent infection and is endemic in rural areas of Malaysia. Against this diagnosis is no preceding colitis (one third) and Entamoeba do not grow on blood or MacConkey agar as they require supplemented media (usually egg yolk). Melioidosis, caused by B. pseudomallei , is a condition causing large abscesses. B. pseudomallei is an environmental saprophyte found in aquatic environments and when cultured grows as mucoid colonies. Going against this as a diagnosis is that infections are most prevalent following the rainy season (rather than summer months when the patient traveled). Also, while it can be found in Malaysia is it more prevalent in Thailand and North Australia. Furthermore, B. pseudomallei are oxidase-positive. Streptococcus intermedius is one of the S. milleri group, which are well recognized as causing deep-seated abscesses such as this. However, the colonial appearances on blood agar are not consistent with S. intermedius, and MacConkey agar does not support its growth. (Image ( left) reprinted with permission from Elsevier. The Lancet. From Prokesch BC, et al. Primary osteomyelitis caused by hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae. Lancet Infect Dis. 2016;16(9):e190–e195. Image ( right) from Rath S, Padhy RN. Prevalence of two multidrug-resistant Klebsiella species in an Indian teaching hospital and adjoining community. J Infect Public Health. 2014;7(6):496–507.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q20

questions.stem: An Escherichia coli isolate is submitted for susceptibility testing. It is resistant to ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and aztreonam, and susceptible to cefoxitin, cefepime, ertapenem, piperacillin/tazobactam, and ciprofloxacin.
questions.lead_in: This pattern is suggestive of drug resistance mediated by what mechanism?
questions.explanation: ESBL Extended-spectrum β-lactamases confer resistance to thirdgeneration cephalosporins but not cephamycins or drugs containing β-lactamase inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with 3 days of diarrhea and severe abdominal pain. She was living in Texas but had traveled to Mexico to visit family 2 weeks prior to presentation. The patient reported drinking raw milk routinely and had a 3-year-old daughter in daycare. Investigations: Multiplex gastrointestinal panel PCR: positive for Shiga toxin 2
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Monitor for development of HUS Although E. coli O157 is the serotype most commonly associated with HUS, any serotype can cause HUS. There is no reason to rule out O157 since the patient should be monitored for HUS regardless of serotype. The presence of Shiga toxin 1 or Shiga toxin 2 is indicative of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), not Shigella. If Shigella was present, it would have been detected as Shigella. A Shigella-specific target is part of all currently available GI panels. Antimicrobial treatment of STEC has historically been associated with worse outcomes. There are some newer data that refute this dogma, but the standard practice is still to avoid antimicrobials for STEC.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q1

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presented in status epilepticus. He was usually fit and well and had returned 1 week earlier from a 2-month visit to Taiwan to visit family. He had no history of recent hospital admission or attendance. He did not take any regular medications, nor did he use any recreational drugs. On examination he had a temperature of 38.3°C, and his pulse was 110 beats/minute. He was sedated, intubated, and transferred to critical care following an urgent CT scan with contrast. Empirical treatment with ceftriaxone and metronidazole was commenced. Investigations: White cell count 23.1 ×109/L (4–11) Neutrophil count 21.8 ×109/L (2–7.5) C-reactive protein 245 mg/L (0–5) Alkaline phosphatase 197 U/L (40–129) ALT 50 U/L (0–41) Total bilirubin 13 μmol/L (0–21) CT head: Liver USS: The liver is heterogenous and mildly enlarged. In the left lobe there is a 79 × 71 × 58mm well-circumscribed, heterogenous area with no vascularity; ? liver abscess
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumoniae The patient has both cerebral abscesses (ring-enhancing lesions) and a liver abscess. There is a systemic inflammatory response with fever, neutrophilia, and raised C-reactive protein. There is a recognized association of primary liver abscesses caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae with hematogenous spread leading to cerebral abscesses. The travel history should be elicited as there is a higher incidence in SE Asia. (Image from Prayson RA, Neuropathology, 2nd ed. Saunders; 2012.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q3

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with cholangitis and a liver abscess. The abscess was aspirated and cultures grew Enterobacter aerogenes. The isolate was reported to be susceptible to ceftriaxone, and so he was started on that agent. He clinically improved over the next few days but then began to have recurrent fevers, and his liver abscess had reaccumulated when his abdominal imaging was repeated. A percutaneous drain was placed and cultures again grew Enterobacter aerogenes, though now resistant to ceftriaxone.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely mechanism of antibiotic resistance reflected in the different susceptibility profiles?
questions.explanation: AmpC induction Some bacteria, most notably some Enterobacteriaceae, have chromosomally determined ampC β-lactamases that can be expressed at high levels after exposure to β-lactams. This can cause clinical failure even if an isolate initially seems susceptible in vitro.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q42

questions.stem: An 18-year-old man was reviewed with recurrent fevers. He was known to have relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. He had been treated 6 months earlier for a Mediport infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus epidermidis with cefepime and vancomycin. On this admission he was treated with gentamicin and meropenem for an ESBL-producing Escherichia coli bacteremia. Five days after meropenem was started, he spiked a fever to 38.5°C, and another blood culture was drawn. The blood culture signaled positive after 8 hours, and the Gram stain showed gram-negative rods.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia S. maltophilia is one of the few bacteria intrinsically resistant to meropenem. It is also intrinsically resistant to gentamicin. Malignancy and exposure to broad-spectrum antimicrobials, especially carbapenems, are risk factors for S. maltophilia infection. Meropenem is effective against ESBLs and wild-type B. cepacia, M. morganii, and P. aeruginosa. Gentamicin is effective against wild-type B. cepacia, M. morganii, and P. aeruginosa and some ESBLs. While any of those organisms can develop resistance to meropenem, the exposure to meropenem was fairly limited, and acquired meropenem resistance is uncommon in pediatrics.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q1

questions.question: A multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacillus produces a carbapenemase that is inhibited by EDTA.
questions.question_raw: MDR GNB with carbepenemase inhibited by EDTA.

parts.text: What is the class of carbapenemase?
In what other organism has it been identified?
What are two non-carbapenemase mechanisms of resistance?

parts_raw.text: A.  What is the class?
B.  What other organism has it been identified in?
C.  What are two non-carbepenemase resistance mechanisms?

questions.model_answer:
a) Metallo-beta-lactamase (Ambler class B). These are zinc-dependent enzymes, hence inhibition by the zinc chelator EDTA; examples include IMP, VIM, and NDM-1.
b) Beyond Enterobacterales (e.g. Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli), metallo-beta-lactamases are found in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii (also Serratia, and environmental Stenotrophomonas maltophilia carries an intrinsic MBL, L1).
c) (1) Porin loss/reduced outer-membrane permeability (e.g. loss of OprD in Pseudomonas) limiting drug entry. (2) Upregulation of efflux pumps actively extruding the drug. (A further non-carbapenemase mechanism is PBP target-site alteration.)

Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter baumanii, Enterobacteriaceae, Serratia

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Place all symptomatic residents on contact precautions in a single room with a dedicated toilet/commode, or cohort them; restrict movement between units and suspend group activities and communal dining. (2) Send stool for culture and Shiga toxin testing on all symptomatic residents, conduct active case finding on every unit, and avoid antimotility agents and antibiotics because of HUS risk.
b) (1) Reinforce and audit hand hygiene with soap and water and adherence to contact precautions; provide education and dedicated PPE at point of care. (2) Exclude symptomatic staff, including food handlers, from work until 48 hours after symptom resolution (and per public health, until clearance stools where required); screen food handlers.
c) (1) Increase frequency of cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces, washrooms and commodes with an appropriate disinfectant. (2) Dedicate toilets/commodes and equipment to affected residents, and review food preparation, storage and water supply with removal of any implicated food.
d) Report to public health immediately and convene an outbreak management team; audit hand hygiene and environmental cleaning compliance with feedback and review kitchen/food-handling practices (HACCP audit).
e) A propagated (person-to-person) outbreak: an initial small point-source cluster followed by successive waves of cases separated by roughly one incubation period, spreading across all units over a month.
f) About 3–4 days (range 1–10 days).
g) Very low infectious dose (fewer than 100 organisms), permitting efficient fecal–oral person-to-person spread.
h) Elderly, often incontinent and cognitively impaired residents with reduced gastric acidity, no pre-existing immunity, and dependence on shared caregivers in a congregate setting.

Employees: Education/reinforce standard precautions including hand washing; Adherence to contact precautions; Staff with diarrhea should stay home until resolved. Environmental: Disinfect surfaces/rooms often; Private toilet for patients with diarrhea. Epi curve: Disseminated outbreak originating from index case with propagated spread (2-hump curve suggests person-to-person transmission). Incubation period: 7d. parts_raw.text: Describe the laboratory method/test to detect the presence of an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) in this organism

The lab technician is worried that this could be a metallo-beta-lactamase. Based on the information you have, give 1 reason why a metallo-beta-lactamase is NOT this strain's mechanism of resistance to beta-lactams

questions.model_answer:
a) Phenotypic confirmation by demonstrating clavulanate inhibition. Screen with ceftazidime and/or cefotaxime (screen positive if MIC >1 mcg/mL or reduced zone). Confirm by combination disk/MIC testing: test cefotaxime and ceftazidime alone versus each combined with clavulanic acid 4 mcg/mL on the same Mueller-Hinton plate. A >=5 mm increase in zone diameter (or a >=3 twofold-dilution, i.e. >=8-fold, decrease in MIC) with clavulanate confirms ESBL production. The double-disk synergy (keyhole) test - a 3rd-generation cephalosporin disk placed 20-30 mm from amoxicillin-clavulanate, with zone extension toward the clavulanate disk - is an equivalent method; molecular detection of blaCTX-M/SHV/TEM can confirm.
b) The isolate is susceptible to meropenem and resistant to aztreonam - the opposite of the metallo-beta-lactamase phenotype. Class B MBLs hydrolyse carbapenems (meropenem would be resistant) but do not hydrolyse the monobactam aztreonam (which would test susceptible unless a separate ESBL/AmpC is present).
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI M100 ESBL confirmatory criteria (>=5 mm zone increase / >=3 twofold dilution decrease with clavulanate).

cohort_answer.text: ESBL detection: Double disk diffusion comparing a 3rd gen cephalosporin and a 3rd gen cephalosporin + beta lactamase inhibitor; ≥5mm difference is a positive screen for ESBL. (Additional notes: K. pneumoniae/E. coli without carbapenemases typically have imipenem/meropenem MICs <0.5 mcg/mL; overt carbapenem resistance in these species raises suspicion for carbapenemase; certain patterns in other Enterobacteriaceae (e.g. S to 3rd gen cephalosporins, R to imipenem) suggest SMC/NMC/IMI enzymes in Serratia/Enterobacter; P. aeruginosa/A. baumannii can be carbapenem-resistant without a carbapenemase, but Aztreonam susceptibility with high carbapenem/cephalosporin/penicillin resistance suggests an MBL.) Reason MBL is NOT the mechanism here: 1. Meropenem is sensitive. 2. Aztreonam is resistant. (Class B metallo-beta-lactamases are typically R to 3rd gen cephalosporin, S to Aztreonam, R to Cefoxitin, R to Clavulin - the opposite pattern.)

questions.model_answer: EHEC produces Shiga toxin (Stx1/Stx2), whose pentameric B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide on host cells; after endocytosis the A subunit depurinates 28S rRNA, halting protein synthesis and triggering inflammation and apoptosis. Toxin binds leukocytes and disseminates in blood, intoxicating endothelial cells (notably renal), increasing procoagulant expression and provoking microvascular thrombosis. The resulting thrombotic microangiopathy causes mechanical hemolysis, platelet consumption/thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

questions.model_answer:
a) EHEC produces Shiga toxin (Stx1/Stx2). The pentameric B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on endothelial cells, which are highly concentrated in the renal glomerulus; after endocytosis the A subunit depurinates 28S rRNA, halting host protein synthesis and injuring endothelium. This triggers inflammation/apoptosis, procoagulant expression, and platelet-fibrin microthrombi (thrombotic microangiopathy) producing the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.
b) (1) Extremes of age, especially children <5 years (and the elderly). (2) Antibiotic therapy (cellular stress, e.g. from fluoroquinolones/TMP, induces high Shiga-toxin levels). (3) Use of antimotility agents.
c) (1) Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on peripheral smear. (2) Thrombocytopenia. (3) Acute kidney injury (rising creatinine/azotemia).

cohort_answer.text:
EHEC produces STX1 or STX2 toxins which bind GB3 receptors in endothelial cells, highly concentrated in renal tissue. These recruit leukocytes, can prompt apoptosis, elicit formation of microthrombi and impaired fibrinolysis; may also have secondary activation of complement

questions.model_answer:
a) The modified Hodge test detects carbapenemase production: a carbapenem-hydrolyzing isolate streaked toward a meropenem/ertapenem disk allows the susceptible E. coli ATCC 25922 lawn to grow inward, producing a cloverleaf-shaped indentation of the zone. Isolate 1 - positive (known carbapenemase-producing control, cloverleaf distortion). Isolate 2 - negative control (straight, undistorted zone edge). Isolate 3 - test isolate, positive, with cloverleaf indentation, consistent with carbapenemase production.
b) AmpC hyperproduction (or ESBL production) combined with outer-membrane porin loss - and/or efflux pump overexpression - giving carbapenem non-susceptibility without a carbapenemase.

cohort_answer.text: MHT detects carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae via cloverleaf-like indentation. In this example: isolate 1 positive test control, isolate 2 negative test control, isolate 3 test isolate - positive for carbapenemase. Alternative mechanism for E. cloacae: Efflux pump or Porin loss (most common) or combined AmpC overexpression and porin loss

questions.model_answer: (1) Shiga toxin production (Stx1/Stx2, phage-encoded); the pentameric B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on host cells and, after endocytosis, the A subunit depurinates 28S rRNA, halting protein synthesis and killing the cell. (2) Endothelial injury and dissemination - Shiga toxin binds leukocytes and is carried in the bloodstream to intoxicate endothelial cells (Gb3-rich renal endothelium), increasing procoagulant expression. (3) Microvascular thrombosis producing a thrombotic microangiopathy with the triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. questions.model_answer:
(1) K. pneumoniae/meropenem: carbapenemase production - Ambler class A KPC (most common), class B metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP), class D OXA-48-type; also ESBL/AmpC plus porin loss (OmpK35/OmpK36).
(2) P. aeruginosa/meropenem: loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (with basal AmpC); acquired metallo-beta-lactamases (VIM, IMP); upregulated MexAB-OprM efflux (affects mero/dori but not imipenem).
(3) E. faecium/penicillin: overproduction of a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 (altered target).
(4) E. faecalis/high-level aminoglycoside resistance: acquired aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme, classically the bifunctional AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia.
(5) S. pneumoniae/moxifloxacin: stepwise target mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining regions of gyrA (DNA gyrase) and parC (topoisomerase IV).
(6) S. pyogenes/erythromycin: ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA by an erm-encoded methylase (MLSB phenotype), or macrolide efflux via mef.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mechanisms are from Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance) / standard microbiology, not this Enterobacteriaceae chapter.

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance. Name the resistance mechanism(s) involved in each scenario: (a) Enterobacter - ceftazidime resistant, cefotaxime resistant, piperacillin-tazobactam resistant, imipenem susceptible; (b) Escherichia coli - ampicillin resistant, cefazolin susceptible, cephalothin intermediate; (c) Pseudomonas - imipenem/meropenem resistant, piperacillin-tazobactam/ceftazidime susceptible; (d) Pseudomonas - imipenem resistant MIC=64, imipenem MIC with EDTA in agar=0.5.
questions.question_raw: Q49 (2008). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism(s) involved: a) Enterobacter - CTZ (R), CTX (R), PipTazo (R), Imipenem (S); b) E coli - Amp (R), Cefazolin (S), Cephalothin (I); c) Pseudomonas - Imi/Mero (R), PipTazo/CTZ (S); d) Pseudomonas - Imipenem (R) MIC=64, MIC with EDTA in agar=0.5

parts.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario.

parts_raw.text: State the resistance mechanism for each scenario

questions.model_answer:
a) Derepression (stable hyperproduction) of the inducible chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (Ambler class C); carbapenem-sparing because AmpC does not hydrolyze imipenem.
b) Broad-spectrum penicillinase (Ambler class A, e.g., TEM-1/SHV-1) - hydrolyzes ampicillin but not cefazolin.
c) Selective carbapenem resistance with retained anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam activity indicates loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (with basal AmpC); an efflux component may coexist.
d) Metallo-beta-lactamase (Ambler class B) - the dramatic fall in imipenem MIC in the presence of the zinc chelator EDTA is diagnostic of a zinc-dependent carbapenemase.
questions.beyond_mandell: Enterobacter chromosomal AmpC derepression is described in this chapter (p. 2682); the Pseudomonas porin-loss and metallo-beta-lactamase mechanisms are from Ch. 18/standard microbiology.

cohort_answer.text: a) De-repression of chromosomal AmpC beta-lactamase (class C) in presence of beta-lactams. b) SHV beta-lactamase (class A). c) OprD porin loss (efflux pump would also likely render resistant to tazo/ceftaz). d) Metallo-beta-lactamase (class B).

E coli R cefoxitin, S PTZ, S carbapenem, S ceftazidime - mechanism?

questions.model_answer: a) Loss/mutation of the OprD porin channel: OprD admits carbapenems but not other beta-lactams, so its loss produces carbapenem resistance while sparing piperacillin-tazobactam. b) An AmpC-type cephalosporinase: resistance to cefoxitin (a cephamycin, not protected by tazobactam) is the hallmark of AmpC, while the low expression here leaves piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, and carbapenems active.
questions.beyond_mandell: The E. coli AmpC interpretation is established Enterobacterales resistance knowledge; this chapter covers Pseudomonas, not E. coli.

cohort_answer.text: Pseudomonas: OprD porin mutation (does not cause Piptazo resistance). E. coli: unclear/possibly misremembered stem; discussion suggests possible TEM-1/SHV-1 or AmpC, though the given susceptibility pattern is inconsistent with classic AmpC or ESBL patterns.
